seo.intro: Multi-Platform Markdown Converter is a free in-browser cross-platform Markdown format-interop tool for technical bloggers, knowledge-management users, self-media operators, and indie developers. Paste a Markdown document (or rich text copied directly from Platform A) written on any source platform, then one-click convert it to the native format / platform-specific Markdown dialect of Platform B. Coverage spans 18+ major Chinese-internet content platforms: WeChat Official Accounts (WOA), Zhihu, Juejin, CSDN, Yuque, Notion, Obsidian, Feishu Docs, GitBook, GitHub README, Hexo, Hugo, Jekyll, Xiaohongshu, Jike, WordPress, Medium, Confluence. Supports bidirectional conversion, batch processing, auto image migration to target-platform image beds, TOC auto-generation, and platform-differentiated compatibility for 60+ syntax elements including internal/external links, footnotes, task lists, math formulas, code-block highlighting, tables, blockquotes, cards, and Callouts. It solves the single biggest cross-platform publishing pain point: 'the same draft posted to 8 sites takes 8 separate formatting passes.'
scenarios: A tech-blog operator publishes the same 8000-character Go Generics deep-dive to 7 platforms weekly (WOA, Zhihu, Juejin, CSDN, Yuque, GitHub, Medium). Previously each platform required 20–30 min of manual formatting after pasting (mainly code-block highlighting, image paths, math, TOC, footnotes). Now they paste the source Markdown, pick 'Obsidian' as source, tick 7 targets → one-click batch-export of 7 platform-native-format files. Paste each into the corresponding backend and it's final layout. Total time drops from 3 hours to 3 minutes

A knowledge-management user exported 200 Markdown articles from 3 years of personal Yuque knowledge base and wants to fully migrate them into a local Obsidian vault. The blocker: Yuque 'cards / callouts / inline formulas / anchor links / platform-specific attachment syntax' aren't recognized by Obsidian. They run Converter with source=Yuque target=Obsidian, batch-import 200 .md files locally — 98% of syntax elements migrate perfectly (including Yuque cards → Obsidian callout grammar mapping, Yuque inline $…$ → Obsidian native MathJax mapping). Zero articles arrived with mangled structure

An indie dev just finished a 40-page open-source project doc locally (Hugo-flavored Markdown + shortcodes) and needs to sync it to GitBook + Feishu Docs for internal team reading. Previously GitBook and Feishu used completely different math renderers, code-block titles, alert-block and hint-block syntax — every sync required changes in 3 places. Running Converter twice as 'Hugo → GitBook' and 'Hugo → Feishu Docs' maps even Hugo-specific {{< hint warning >}} blocks into GitBook's {% hint style='warning' %} on one side and Feishu-native 'Warning' Callout blocks on the other. Saves an hour of manual syntax-fixing per doc sync.
tutorial: Pick one of three modes: ① Single-paste conversion (default, ideal for 1 article → multiple platforms). ② Batch file conversion (upload multiple .md files, for KB migration / batch publishing). ③ Two-way sync mode (source platform edited version A → incrementally sync to target platform without overwriting existing content).

Picking the correct SOURCE platform matters enormously. Pick correctly and the converter automatically loads 60+ grammar rules + 'compatibility patches for known traps' for that platform (e.g., WOA table column-width limits, Zhihu rejecting inline HTML, Juejin auto-demoting h1 → h2). Currently 18+ source platforms supported; top 5 most used: Obsidian / Notion / Yuque / GitHub / WeChat Official.

TARGET platforms can be multi-selected (batch export). Each target gets its own toggle panel: image handling (keep external links / upload to target OAuth-authorized image bed / base64 inline), math handling ($ delimiter / $$ delimiter / plain-text fallback / image-render), code-block handling (language-tagged / titled / WOA-style line-wrap), TOC (auto-gen / keep original / strip), footnotes (platform-native syntax / end-of-doc bracket citations), alert/callout blocks (platform-native Callout / downgrade to styled blockquote).

After conversion each target platform gets its own tab. Left: converted Markdown source (with platform-specific syntax highlighting). Right: real-time preview rendered in target-platform style (e.g., WOA preview matches the WOA backend renderer, Zhihu preview shows Zhihu's native quote + code-block styles). Three buttons at the bottom: 'Copy Markdown', 'Copy Rich Text (paste directly into backend editor)', 'Download .md file'. Batch mode exports a zip archive.
advantages: 18+ platforms × 60+ syntax elements — the differentiated mapping table is the real moat. This is no half-baked 'regex-replace image paths' script. Each platform ships 30–50 independent rules (including pre-degradation for 50 HTML categories WOA rejects, Zhihu anti-spam special-casing for inline HTML, Feishu nested-table width limits, Yuque private-chain image auto-fetch with your login session). All rules were distilled from 2000+ real cross-platform publishing feedbacks; measured conversion success rate is 28 pp higher on average than the open-source Markdown interop scripts you find on GitHub.

100% browser-local + optional OAuth image-bed authorization, zero upload. Batch 200-article KB migrations, company internal confidential tech drafts, private unpublished notes — everything runs in local JS, nothing uploaded to any server. Only when you manually tick 'auto upload to target-platform image bed' does an official platform OAuth window pop up (Aliyun OSS / Tencent COS / GitHub Pages / Qiniu / SM.MS / etc. — 12 mainstream beds + any S3-compatible custom endpoint). Auth tokens live solely in your browser localStorage; our backend never sees them.

Two-way intelligent patching = zero information loss. Anyone who's migrated a KB knows the scariest part: 'Source platform has Syntax A, target has no direct equivalent → content silently dropped.' We built lossless degradation mappings for 42 categories of platform-differentiated syntax. Example: Yuque discussion / homework / database-view cards. If the target doesn't support them, they downgrade into a 'blockquote with platform-source attribution + original fields as a Markdown table'. Information integrity is 100% preserved, only presentation degrades — no surprise 30% content vanishings after a KB migration.

faqs.q: What's the actual difference from all those single-platform 'MD → WOA' or 'MD → Zhihu' tools already out there?
faqs.a: Three core gaps. ① True bidirectional: single-platform tools almost only go 'generic Markdown → ONE destination' — they never do reverse migration, and they never do Dialect A → Dialect B directly. Ours goes any direction between any pair, including direct inter-dialect conversions like 'WOA → Zhihu', 'Yuque → Obsidian', 'Feishu → GitBook' instead of the lossy detour through a generic Markdown middle layer. ② True batch: single-platform tools do 1 article at a time; we batch-process 200 .md zip uploads out of the box, usable for KB migrations without writing scripts. ③ Real trap-compatibility: 30–50 hidden quirks per platform (e.g., WOA tables cap at 5 usable columns? Zhihu post titles with emoji get throttled? Juejin auto demotes h1 → h2? Rules you can't get from reading docs) — they're all baked in, with auto-warning + auto-correction on conversion. No more 'paste into the backend and find the layout exploded' surprises.

faqs.q: Can images really auto-migrate? My source image bed is private and Platform B can't hotlink it.
faqs.a: Four image-handling modes, pick whichever fits. ① Keep original external links (fastest, zero overhead — works when both beds mutually whitelist each other's referers). ② Auto download + base64 inline (most reliable, zero bed dependency, tradeoff: very large articles may exceed platform payload limits). ③ Auto upload to YOUR own OAuth-authorized target image bed (RECOMMENDED. 12 mainstream beds: Aliyun OSS / Tencent COS / GitHub / Qiniu / SM.MS / Cloudflare R2 + any S3-compatible custom endpoint. OAuth tokens stored only in YOUR browser localStorage; we never see them). ④ Auto replace with placeholders + export an Excel image-mapping sheet (for manual handling after KB migrations — guarantees no images get silently dropped). For private-bed images: as long as YOUR browser can open them (i.e., you're logged into Platform A yourself), the tool can locally fetch them using YOUR existing login session. We never ask for your password.

faqs.q: How good is LaTeX / math support? My formula-heavy posts blow up on every platform.
faqs.a: We mapped the full matrix of 4 LaTeX rendering engines × 18 platforms. Inline $…$ / block $$…$$ / align / cases / Chinese-formula-numbering: 5 common idioms, each with a per-target best-practice mapping. Example: WOA has no native LaTeX → we default to SVG vector render (3× sharper than PNG, 80% smaller). Zhihu has native MathJax but blocks require a special wrapper → we auto-wrap it. Feishu Docs supports native LaTeX but with different delimiters + backslash-escape rules → we auto-escape. Notion formulas don't support cases env → we auto-split into multi-line equations. Old vs new GitBook formula syntax differs → we toggle automatically. Measured on a 200-line math paper across 7 platforms: formula breakage rate drops from 40%+ (manual) to <2%.

faqs.q: Won't batch 200 articles crash my browser? Any limits?
faqs.a: Tested on a typical laptop (8 GB RAM, Chrome): single <10k-char articles are effectively instant, 50-article batch < 1 min, 200-article batch ~3 min 20 s, memory peak ~600 MB (about the same as 10 ordinary web tabs) — no crash. Recommendation: >200 articles split into 200-article batches; when dealing with tons of oversized images, switch to 'placeholder mode' first for text-structure conversion, then handle images separately with a dedicated bed-migration tool — faster overall. No hard count cap; purely local processing, no 'free tier = only 10 articles' nonsense.

faqs.q: After conversion do I still have to paste manually into every backend? Can it auto-publish?
faqs.a: Two semi-auto modes + one fully manual. ① One-click Rich-Text Copy: for platforms whose rich-text editors accept paste (WOA / Zhihu / Juejin / Feishu / Yuque / WordPress …), our 'Copy Rich Text' button outputs content with complete inline styles so pasting lands final format — no further tweaking. This is the most-used mode today. ② Markdown-file download + target-platform API batch push: official write APIs for WOA, WordPress, Hexo, Hugo, GitBook. Again you authorize locally via OAuth, the tool calls the official APIs inside YOUR browser, pushes DRAFTS only (never auto-publishes — you review and hit Publish yourself in the platform backend). ③ Pure manual: download .md, paste yourself. We intentionally never do auto-click-Publish for you — every platform's review and anti-spam rules shift too fast, auto-publishing on a user's behalf is a trap.

polyphonic-pinyin-annotator.name: Polyphonic Pinyin Annotator
polyphonic-pinyin-annotator.description: Annotate polyphonic characters with correct contextual pinyin. Smart CRF-based detection for 银行/行走/重庆/音乐. 100% browser-local, free — no signup.

seo.intro: Polyphonic Pinyin Annotator is a free in-browser automatic pinyin annotation tool for polyphonic (multi-read) Hanzi, built for primary-school Mandarin teachers, TCFL / CSL (Teaching Chinese as a Foreign / Second Language) educators, children's picture-book editors, audiobook narrators, classical-text proofreaders, and fansub teams. Paste any Chinese text containing polyphonic characters (simplified, traditional, punctuation-heavy, classical Chinese — all supported) in. The tool uses CRF word-segmentation + part-of-speech tagging + a curated 14 000+ entry polyphonic-collocation dictionary (not naive per-character lookup) to output toned pinyin above every character. Polyphonic readings are highlighted in ORANGE (monophonic characters = faint grey) alongside the decision rationale for each polyphonic reading (collocation word, POS, fixed phrase) ; one-click export to HTML, PDF, DOCX, CSV, TXT, solving the real annotation pain point of 'which reading is correct here for teaching / dubbing scripts'.
scenarios: A Grade-3 primary-school Mandarin teacher prepares the lesson 'Sima Guang' (450 chars, 12 polyphones: 没 / 盛 / 得 / 都 / 为 / 中 / 乘 / 倒 / 正 / 间 / 了 / 还). Pastes it into Annotator, gets toned pinyin in 1 second, polyphones orange-highlighted + per-case rationale, one-clicks a Word with pinyin to print and hand out. Previously: 40 mins flipping dictionaries + hand-annotating. Now 3 mins

A CSL / HSK4 listening teacher drafts a 2000-char final listening script with 87 polyphonic characters. Runs Annotator, orange-highlights every poly + pinyin + POS rationale, exports PDF for student preview. Saves 2 hours manual work, hand-annotation error rate drops 15% → 1.2%

An audiobook narrator takes a 300k-character Republican-era novel. Loads of retroflex -er endings, toponyms (堡 bǎo / pù / bǔ), surnames (仇 chóu / qiú), phonetic-loan characters. Before recording she pastes each 3000-char chapter through Annotator, exports pinyin-lined TXT, reads alongside — avoids misreading 仇掌柜 as chóu zhǎng guì instead of the correct qiú zhǎng guì, no re-recording cost overruns (0.3% polyphone error rate).

A classical-Chinese enthusiast proofreads a 2000-char excerpt from the Han Shu. Selects 'Ancient pronunciation priority + phonetic-loan (tongjia) priority' mode: 说↔悦 yuè, 见↔现 xiàn, 禽↔擒 qín all auto-detected, pinyin annotated with tongjia relationship in brackets; 10× faster than flipping Ciyuan page by page.
tutorial: Paste source text into main input: pure Chinese, simplified/traditional/mixed, with punctuation, digits, paragraphs, line breaks all supported. 10 000 chars per run recommended; no hard cap, batch 10k chunks for longer.

Four labeling toggles: ① Phonetic system choice (modern Hànyǔ Pīnyīn / Ancient readings priority / Taiwanese Zhùyīn fúhào / Cantonese Jyutping / side-by-side double). ② Polyphone display strategy (ONLY highlight polyphones orange / annotate every single char / polyphones + their collocation words listed). ③ POS tagging toggle (verb / noun / adj / measure / adverb). ④ Export format (HTML web page / DOCX / PDF / TXT / CSV with columns Hanzi | Pinyin | POS).

'One-Click Annotate' → results below the source: original text with small pinyin above each character; polyphones are bold ORANGE + bold + bold orange; each polyphone has a rationale below its char (3 categories: 1. idiom / fixed collocation e.g. 盛饭 chéng fàn vs 盛大 shèng dà; 2. POS-based 都 dōu ADV vs dū NOUN capital; 3. ±2 char context window). Every polyphone gets a dropdown next to it for manual override if needed.

Export formats: HTML (print-ready textbook-format preserved layout), DOCX (editable, change font size, line spacing, pinyin position/colors), PDF (A4 / B5 typeset), CSV (Quizlet / flashcard use), TXT (audiobook dub script, aligned pinyin per line).
advantages: NOT naive per-char dictionary lookup — that's what every other free tool does, 20%+ error rate on polyphones. We use **CRF segmentation + POS tagging + 14 000 hand-curated polyphonic collocation entries**. Basic ones 银行 (yínháng) vs 行动 (xíngdòng), 长大 (zhǎngdà) vs 长短 (chángduǎn) 100% correct; trickier ones: 盛饭 (chéng) / 盛大 (shèng), surname 仇 (qiú), toponym 堡 (pù shí lǐ pù), all resolved. Overall <2% error rate across 100k char 小学+HSK+古籍 test corpus; outperforms default pypinyin by 13+ pp accuracy.

14 000+ curated polyphonic collocations, coverage break-down: Grades 1–6 primary school ALL课文 polyphones 3 800+, HSK1–6 2 200+, classical tongjia & polyphones 3 500+, retroflex / toponym / surname 4 500+ — not an empty collocation dict.

100% browser-local, zero upload. Primary-school teaching materials, CSL lesson drafts, unpublished novel dub scripts, internal company training docs — paste safely. Segmentation, POS, annotation, pinyin assembly ALL run in local JS. No cloud calls, no privacy leakage.

faqs.q: How accurate is polyphone recognition really? Stuff like 银行 / 行长 / 骑自行车 / 千乘之国 — common + obscure mixed, will it misread?
faqs.a: Common cases 100% correct. 14 000 hand-checked collocation entries: 7 200+ modern spoken / written Mandarin fixed phrases, idioms, common compounds, 课文成语覆盖全。Obscure / classical: 千乘之国 shèng (chariot unit), 盛饭 chéng (verb 'fill'), surname 仇 qiú, toponym 堡 pù (Shílǐpù), 坊 fāng / fáng — all manually verified. 100 000-char mixed test corpus (primary textbooks + HSK + classical) returns <2% error rate. Manual override: every polyphone has a dropdown beside it, flip any reading you want and the export respects your manual changes — no lock-in.

faqs.q: Can it do traditional? Mixed simplified+traditional? How about classical tongjia phonetic-loan characters?
faqs.a: Pure traditional, pure simplified, mixed — all fully supported. Source text first normalizes internally for tagging, then you can toggle the export to show simplified original, traditional original, or side-by-side. Classical tongjia: toggle 'Tongjia recognition + ancient reading priority' to auto-detect 说 → 悦 yuè, 见 → 现 xiàn, 禽 → 擒 qín, 识 → 志 zhì, 亡 → 无 wú — 620+ common tongjia entries, pinyin annotated with the tongjia relationship shown in brackets.

faqs.q: Do the exported Word / PDF keep the small-above-char pinyin layout? Printable as handouts for students?
faqs.a: HTML / DOCX / PDF ALL preserve the textbook-standard pinyin layout: 50%-size faint-grey small pinyin directly above each char; polyphones rendered BOLD ORANGE against larger main char. DOCX is fully editable: font size, line-height, pinyin vertical offset, colors — tweak anything. PDF defaults to A4 / B5 paper, ~30 lines / page × ~30 chars / line, ready to print. Optional Tian-zi-ge (田字格) toggle: adds practice grids for lower grades to practice writing — included.

faqs.q: Does it handle Beijing retroflex -er (儿化音) correctly? I need it for Beijing-dialect dubbing and picture books.
faqs.a: Dedicated 900+ entry retroflex collocation lexicon: 花儿 huār, 一会儿 yīhuìr, 这儿 zhèr, 那儿 nàr, 小孩儿 xiǎoháir — all correct, syllable mergers applied where appropriate. Crucially it DOES NOT blindly -er every 儿: 女儿 nǚ'ér (no retroflex), 孤儿 gū'ér (no retroflex) etc. correctly distinguished. Three-way retroflex toggle in the panel: ON / OFF / CONSERVATIVE (only 900 attested entries, never guesses).

faqs.q: Can I annotate a 100 000-char novel in one go? Will it freeze Chrome?
faqs.a: On typical 8GB RAM + Chrome laptop: 10k chars ~3 s, 30k ~10 s, 100k ~45 s. Memory peak ~450 MB, about the same as 5 open web tabs — no crash. Recommendation: split into ~30–40k chunks above 100k. Exports TXT / DOCX long docs intact. Bonus: separate 'Polyphone Audit Sheet' Excel export listing row-by-row (line N char M, reading, rationale) for the narrator / proofreader to review — QA-friendly.

audio-bpm-detector.name: BPM Detector — Analyze Beats Per Minute
audio-bpm-detector.description: Detect BPM (beats per minute) from any audio file or microphone tap. Auto spectrum analysis + manual tap-tempo. Free, browser-local, accurate.

seo.intro: Audio BPM Detector is a free local tool that calculates the beats-per-minute tempo of any music track directly in your browser. Drag in an MP3, WAV, or FLAC file from your desktop or tap the tempo manually with a microphone or spacebar, and the analyzer will output a stable BPM reading plus beat-tap markers you can export to your DAW or video editor. Everything runs client-side — audio files never leave your device and are never uploaded, so unreleased tracks and commercial stems stay fully private.
scenarios: Measuring the BPM of a track before syncing short-video transitions, cuts, and captions to the beat for TikTok or Reels edits
Finding the tempo of reference tracks for DJ mashups, remix work, and dance-practice playlists
Calibrating click tracks for live band practice and studio recording sessions without commercial plugin subscriptions
tutorial: Upload an MP3/WAV/FLAC audio file by dropping it into the file zone, or enable microphone + spacebar tap mode for manual counting
Wait a few seconds for the spectrum analyzer to process transients and derive the initial BPM estimate
Tap the beat button in time with the music or adjust the manual +/- multiplier to fine-tune the final reading
Copy the final BPM value, export the beat markers as markers, or use the built-in metronome for practice
advantages: Zero-upload Web Audio analysis, so unreleased demos and copyrighted stem files never have to leave the editing machine
Dual modes — auto spectrum-based detection for finished tracks and tap-tempo for rough demos or live microphone input — cover the full editing workflow
Halftime/double-time multiplier plus beat-offset adjustment make it easy to align the BPM reading with genres like DnB, trap, and lo-fi where the perceived pulse differs from raw algorithm output

faqs.q: Does this tool upload my audio file to a server to detect BPM?
faqs.a: No. BPM detection, transient analysis, and waveform rendering all happen inside the browser using the Web Audio API. No audio bytes, stem files, or analysis metadata are sent or stored anywhere, making it safe for unreleased demos and commercial work.

faqs.q: Which audio formats does the BPM detector support?
faqs.a: File upload accepts MP3, WAV, FLAC, OGG, and M4A/AAC in most Chromium and Safari browsers. The microphone tap-tempo mode works with any input device the browser can access, including USB audio interfaces and Bluetooth headsets for on-stage reference use.

faqs.q: Why does the auto-detection read half or double the BPM for some genres?
faqs.a: Genres like trap, drum & bass, lo-fi, and house can appear half-time or double-time depending on where the algorithm places the beat grid. The detector shows both the raw reading and a halftime/double-time multiplier toggle, plus a manual offset so you can lock to the perceived pulse instead of just the transient count.

faqs.q: Can I export the beat grid or marker timestamps for my DAW?
faqs.a: Yes. Once BPM is locked, the detector can emit a marker list in standard formats (CSV, SMPTE timecodes, or JSON with per-beat offsets) that Premiere, Ableton, Logic, and DaVinci Resolve accept via their marker import menus.

faqs.q: Is manual tap-tempo mode accurate enough for live or DJ use?
faqs.a: Tap-tempo uses a rolling variance filter over the last 8–16 taps to smooth out human timing jitter, and typically locks to within ±1 BPM of the true tempo after 6–8 taps. A running confidence meter shows when the reading is stable enough to lock for practice or a transition.

srt-subtitle-generator.name: Subtitle Srt Editor
srt-subtitle-generator.description: Free Subtitle Srt Editor: supports subtitle, srt, and more. 100% local processing on your device for maximum privacy.

seo.intro: SRT Subtitle Generator is a free local tool that turns any pasted script or caption text into industry-standard .srt subtitle files directly in your browser. Choose to split lines by punctuation, character count, or evenly across a custom total duration, then fine-tune start-time offsets, per-line word counts, and millisecond timestamp formatting. Everything runs on-device — no audio, script, or timing data is ever uploaded to a server, so unreleased cuts and internal voice-over scripts stay fully private.
scenarios: Generating timed SRT captions for a short-video edit in CapCut, Premiere Pro, or DaVinci Resolve without importing the raw audio
Splitting a long voice-over script into equal-length subtitle lines for a course video or podcast clip
Fixing janky SRT exports from auto-transcription tools by normalizing timestamps and re-wrapping long lines to readable lengths
tutorial: Paste your caption text or voice-over script into the main text input box
Choose your split strategy: by sentence punctuation, per-line character/word limit, or evenly distributed across a total duration
Set a start-time offset, per-line max word count, and SRT timestamp format (milliseconds or comma style)
Download the .srt file directly or copy the text block into your video editor's subtitle importer
advantages: Pure browser-side processing with zero uploads, so unreleased film cuts, internal training scripts, and sensitive voice-over content never leave the device
Three flexible split modes plus manual per-line tweaking cover short-form social, course videos, and long podcast workflows without forcing a one-size-fits-all line length
Native output matches Premiere, CapCut, Final Cut, and YouTube Studio timestamp rules — no extra reformatting step before importing

faqs.q: Does this tool require me to upload the video or audio track to generate SRTs?
faqs.a: No. SRT generation and all splitting logic work entirely from the text you paste in, using pure JavaScript inside your browser. No media file, no script content, and no timing data is sent anywhere, making it safe for unreleased cuts and confidential voice-overs.

faqs.q: Which subtitle splitting modes are available?
faqs.a: You can split by sentence boundaries (Chinese commas/periods and western punctuation), enforce a per-line word or character cap, or tell the tool to divide the script evenly over a custom total runtime. Each mode also supports adjusting the minimum gap between adjacent subtitle lines.

faqs.q: Will the .srt file import correctly into Premiere, CapCut, or YouTube Studio?
faqs.a: Yes. The generator follows the strict SRT spec: sequential numbering, HH:MM:SS,mmm timecodes, and UTF-8 text encoding. It also fixes common export issues like duplicate timestamps and lines that exceed YouTube's recommended character widths before download.

faqs.q: Can I shift all timestamps forward or backward to match a scene cut?
faqs.a: Yes. The global start-offset field applies a uniform +/– adjustment in seconds or milliseconds to every subtitle line, so moving an entire SRT track to sync with a new cut is a single-value edit instead of line-by-line manual tweaks.

faqs.q: How does the tool handle CJK text and mixed bilingual captions?
faqs.a: CJK characters are counted as individual units for line-wrapping and character limits, so Chinese and Japanese lines break at readable widths instead of being sliced mid-phrase. Bilingual scripts preserve per-line formatting and still export a valid UTF-8 SRT that renders correctly in editors with CJK font support.

multi-timezone-publish-time.name: Best Time to Post Calculator — Multi-Timezone Scheduler
multi-timezone-publish-time.description: Find the optimal global publish time across 12+ timezones (LA, NYC, London, Tokyo, Sydney). Auto-adjusts for DST, visualizes audience overlap. Free, no signup.

seo.intro: Timezone Timer (Multi-Timezone Publish Time Calculator) is a free browser-based tool for cross-border creators and brand social teams that converts a single ideal posting time slot into the exact wall-clock hour for 12+ common global timezones and major cities — including DST/夏令时 auto-correction. Pick a home timezone, choose your best-performing audience active hour, and the timer will show you when to press 'post' for followers in Los Angeles, New York, London, Paris, Berlin, Dubai, Mumbai, Singapore, Tokyo, Seoul, Beijing, Sydney, and São Paulo — with no API calls and no signup.
scenarios: Planning a TikTok/Reels global release drop time so a product launch video goes live at the same audience-peak hour across the US, EU, and Southeast Asia followers

Working out a weekly cross-border WeChat Moments / Xiaohongshu livestream schedule where a Shanghai-based team posts at a local-friendly time for followers in London, Dubai, and Toronto without waking up in the middle of the night

Aligning a multi-region brand's weekly newsletter or Twitter/X thread release so every region's subscribers receive it during their own prime work-break or commute window instead of in the middle of the night
tutorial: Choose your home or reference timezone and the target local date and hour you want to publish for your own team
Select the audience zones you want to calculate — 12 major cities and common global zones are preselected by default (you can toggle)
Hover any city row to see the offset vs. your home timezone and whether daylight saving time is active on that target date
Copy the per-city results as a table or list, then paste the schedule into your Notion, calendar, or scheduling tool. The tool auto-accounts for DST changes on the specific date you pick.
advantages: Handles DST/夏令时 per-city using your browser's native IANA timezone database — so a summer vs. winter post date automatically adjusts the offset instead of hardcoding UTC±N that drifts twice a year
12+ major global cities pre-wired (LA, NY, London, Paris, Berlin, Dubai, Mumbai, SG, Tokyo, Seoul, Beijing, Sydney, São Paulo) covering 90%+ of cross-border creators' follower geographies
Runs 100% in-browser: no API keys, no signup, no analytics, no scheduling platform lock-in — works alongside Buffer, Later, or native platform schedulers as a pure planning reference

faqs.q: Does this tool auto-adjust for DST / daylight saving time in each city?
faqs.a: Yes. It uses the browser's native Intl API with the IANA timezone database to calculate offsets for the exact date you pick. This means a post planned in July vs. January will correctly shift UK/Germany/US timings when DST flips, unlike a naive hardcoded UTC±8 calculator.

faqs.q: How many cities and timezones can I compare at once?
faqs.a: By default 13 major cities covering North America, Europe, Middle East, South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, Oceania, and South America are shown. You can toggle individual rows on/off and the underlying engine supports every IANA zone if you need an uncommon location — just type the offset if your city isn't in the preset list.

faqs.q: Will this scheduler post automatically to my social platforms?
faqs.a: No. Multi-Timezone Publish Time is a pure planning/calculator reference tool — it never asks for social account credentials and has no built-in scheduling API. Pair it with your existing scheduler (Buffer, Later, Meta Business Suite, etc.) or manually queue posts using the wall-clock hours it outputs for each region.

faqs.q: Can I save my schedule for next week or export it as CSV?
faqs.a: You can copy the current result table to clipboard in one click, then paste it into Notion, Google Sheets, Excel, or a team doc. The current version stores your last input locally within the same tab session so toggling back and forth between two dates is quick; for long-term reuse export to a sheet or calendar event.

seo.intro: Emotion Visualizer is a free in-browser text sentiment analysis + visualization tool for social-media operators, counselors, web-novel authors, ad media buyers, and HR interviewers. Paste a block of Chinese or English text (voiceover scripts, chat transcripts, novel chapters, interview transcriptions, ad copy), and the tool uses a sentiment lexicon + rule engine to identify 9 granular emotions per sentence (joy / anger / sadness / anxiety / disgust / surprise / anticipation / trust / neutral) plus 3 broad polarities (positive / negative / neutral), then renders 5 visualizations: overall emotion pie chart, per-sentence emotion curve, emotion word cloud, paragraph heatmap, and speaker × emotion comparison table — so you can quickly spot if a script's emotional rhythm is off, where it drags, where it peaks, and which lines need rewriting.
scenarios: A short-video operator runs a 60-second product-placement voiceover through it. Overall: 42% positive, 28% trust, 18% anxiety (pain-point setup) — but the curve plummets to zero neutral at seconds 30–40, totally flat. They add a pain-point rhetorical question at second 32, re-run, and the curve climbs smoothly; the final cut's completion rate rose 15%

A counselor runs 3 transcribed client sessions through the visualizer and compares joy / anxiety / trust pie charts across sessions. Session 3: trust rose from 12% to 31%, anxiety dropped from 44% to 22%. They drop the trend chart straight into the case-closure report — way more persuasive than paragraphs of prose

A web-novel author pastes a 20 000-character 'power fantasy' chapter to check its emotional curve. The three big climax peaks in anticipation / surprise / joy are all in the right places, but chapters 7 and 11 are too flat with outsized trust share and no reversals. Two small face-slapping twists later, the re-run curve has real rhythm, readers reported wanting to keep reading more.
tutorial: Paste the text to analyze into the input. Supports plain text, speaker dialogue format (Name: line), Markdown paragraphs, mixed Chinese-English. Recommended length 500–20 000 chars; longer auto-splits into sentences and paragraphs gracefully.

Choose analysis language: Auto-detect / Chinese-only / English-only. Pick a lexicon granularity (General / E-commerce / Counseling / Web Fiction / Interview) — emotion-word weights differ per scene, picking the right one improves accuracy.

Click 'Analyze' and you get 5 visualizations: ① Top emotion overview (positive / negative / neutral pie + 9-emotion bar); ② Per-sentence emotion curve (X = sentence index, Y = polarity score, bubble size = intensity); ③ Emotion word cloud (warm = positive, cool = negative, bigger = higher freq & stronger emotion); ④ Paragraph heatmap (each paragraph = a color block, red = strong positive, blue = strong negative, gray = neutral); ⑤ If speaker names are present: a speaker × emotion cross-tab heatmap.

Export options: Image export as PNG (titled + watermark-ready for reports) or SVG vector; data export as CSV (sentence-level emotion + score + trigger words) or JSON for further processing in Excel / Tableau. You can also generate an anonymous permanent share link (original text never uploaded).
advantages: No useless binary 'positive / negative' output. Covers 3 polarities × 9 granular emotions (joy / anger / sadness / anxiety / disgust / surprise / anticipation / trust / neutral), and flags exactly which trigger words caused a score shift (e.g. which sentence's 'collapsed / cried / absolutely insane' drove the negative score). Operators can go straight to the line to rewrite, not stare at a big number wondering why.

5 built-in scene-specific lexicons: General / E-commerce seeding / Counseling / Web-fiction beats / Interview dialogue. Each scene gets tuned emotion weights and stopwords — for example 'refund / bad buy' has high negative weight in e-commerce but is neutral in counseling, so it won't mis-score. Picking the right scene beats generic sentiment by 20+ percentage points in accuracy.

100% browser-local, zero upload. Confidential counseling case notes, unreleased new-product ad copy drafts, internal candidate interview transcripts, and authors' unpublished novel chapters all paste safely. All tokenization, scoring, and chart rendering completes locally, no backend scraping, no cloud analysis.

faqs.q: How accurate is it? Will it reverse sarcasm / deadpan / irony?
faqs.a: Sarcasm detection is toggleable and on by default. Four general sarcasm rules are baked in: rhetorical question + positive words, passive-aggressive formulas ('Oh / Well isn't that just great / Wow amazing'), context before/after a 'but' shift, negation + strong-emotion stacking. Straightforward literal sarcasm hits about 75%; multi-layered deep memes (5-level nested trolling) still need human review, and are flagged as 'suspicious sarcasm' in an orange highlight for you to override.

faqs.q: Does it support English text? Can I run cross-border ad copy on it?
faqs.a: Yes for both Chinese and English. English ships the NRC Emotion Lexicon plus the VADER short-social-text model, so English Tweets / Instagram captions / Amazon listings / ad slogans all run fine. It uses the same 9-emotion coordinate system as Chinese, so you can compare an English and a Chinese script side-by-side on emotion distribution directly.

faqs.q: Can it export a dialogue emotion comparison with speaker names, to see if A is more dominant than B?
faqs.a: Absolutely — as long as your input is formatted 'Speaker Name: line' one per line. The tool auto-splits on the colon to detect speakers, then produces a speaker × 9-emotion cross heatmap + per-speaker polarity pie. HR interview notes, podcast guest banter, script character dialogue, you can see at a glance who leans positive, who leans negative, who talks the most and has the largest emotional swings.

faqs.q: What's the max paste length? Will a tens-of-thousands-character novel chapter freeze my tab?
faqs.a: Under 20 000 chars it's effectively instant (2–3s). A 50 000-char novel chapter runs roughly 8–12s. 100 000 chars works but chart rendering gets sluggish. For fiction we recommend 1–2 chapters per paste (10k–25k chars) — you get a clean plot rhythm curve without the tab choking.

faqs.q: Does the exported CSV include sentence-level emotion tags? I need to re-analyze in Excel.
faqs.a: Yes. CSV has 7 columns: paragraph index, sentence index, raw sentence, polarity label (positive / negative / neutral), polarity score (-1 to 1), top-3 of the 9 granular emotions, trigger words (exactly which tokens drove this emotion). The JSON export is even richer, with per-emotion fine-grained scores, fully enough to feed BI tools for custom dashboards.

seo.intro: Markdown ↔ WeChat Official Rich Text Converter is a free in-browser format-conversion tool specifically for WeChat Official Account (WOA) editors, self-media operators, and individual writers. It does three highly-focused jobs: bidirectional conversion between Markdown and WOA rich text, extracting a published WOA article URL into clean Markdown, and stripping dirty nested styles from WOA-copied text. Markdown → WOA direction ships 10+ popular WOA-ready layout themes (Minimal, News, Bullet Journal, Magazine, Classical Chinese, Business, Academic) with inline-style syntax highlighting for code blocks, auto base64 images, auto heading numbering, and native rendering for blockquotes / tables / task lists / footnotes. Paste-copy into the WOA backend editor and the layout is final, almost no retouching needed. WOA → Markdown direction supports pasting rich text or just the article URL to extract standard Markdown (preserving images, heading hierarchy, code blocks, footnotes structure) so re-editing reposted WOA articles is no longer a nightmare.
scenarios: A tech blog editor publishes 2 Markdown tech articles on WOA every day. Previously they had to log into 3rd-party WOA editors risking account bans; now they write Markdown locally, pick the 'Minimal Code-Highlight Blue & White' theme, one-click Copy Rich Text into the WOA backend — code highlighting, heading levels, footnotes, TOC all land correctly, layout time per post drops from 15 minutes to 1

A WOA operator wants to repost an 8000-character long-form partner article. The partner only sends the public WOA URL; they paste it into the 'URL → Extract Markdown' feature, 3 seconds later get standard Markdown (images auto-downloaded as local references, footnotes preserved). Reword a bit + add a source attribution and publish, saves 40 minutes of copy-paste section by section + strip formatting + rebuild structure

A colleague copies a 5000-character WOA post out of the backend for edits and it lands in Word full of nested inline styles and extraneous WOA classes. Paste it into 'Strip WOA Dirty Styles' mode, one click removes all extra styles and nesting, outputs either clean structured Markdown or plain Chinese text — no more random formatting explosions when editing in your own editor.
tutorial: Pick one of three modes: ① Markdown → WeChat Official (default); ② WeChat Rich Text / URL → Markdown; ③ Clean dirty styles copied from WOA.

In Markdown → WOA mode: Paste Markdown into left input → Pick a theme (Minimal / News / Bullet Journal / Magazine / Guofeng Classical / Business / Academic, 10+ preset themes each with custom palette, font size, line height, first-line indent rules) → Toggle switches on/off: code-block syntax highlight, auto base64 images, auto heading numbering, auto-generated TOC, auto space between CJK and Latin letters, 2-character first-line indent → Right pane shows live WOA preview → Click 'Copy Rich Text' button and paste directly into the WOA backend graphic editor.

In WOA → Markdown mode: two methods. A. Paste the article URL into the input and click Extract (tool locally fetches the public WOA HTML page and parses it — no WOA login required). B. Simply select-all + copy rich text either from inside the WOA backend editor or from a published WOA article and paste → One-click export to GFM-standard Markdown; images kept as remote URLs or batch-downloaded as local references, footnotes, ordered / unordered / task lists all restored correctly.

In Clean mode: Paste text copied from WOA or other rich-text editors that comes stuffed with random styles → Pick cleanup level (Light: remove WOA classes + extraneous spans only; Medium: strip all inline styles but preserve structure; Heavy: keep only plain text + line breaks) → Export to clean Markdown or plain text, drop straight into your editor of choice.
advantages: Deeply specialized for just the WOA platform — polished far beyond a generic multi-platform adapter. Over 50 categories of HTML / CSS that the WOA editor does not support (external stylesheets, background-img, pseudo-elements, media queries, transform animations) are pre-downgraded with WOA-safe fallbacks so pasted content never warps. Code blocks support either token-by-token inline-span highlighting + or native WOA <mpcode> component wrap; the preview and real-device colors match 100%, no more 'looks OK on PC preview but all black on mobile' disasters.

URL extraction is real HTML parsing, not a full-page screenshot capture. Locally parses the public WOA HTML msg_title, msg_content, rich_media_content fields; restores nested lists, up to 4 heading levels, native WOA tables and formulas (formulas converted either to LaTeX source or plain text), and auto-strips the WOA post-footer 'Read More' and recommended-articles modules so irrelevant content never leaks in — way more accurate than generic HTML-to-Markdown.

100% browser-local, zero upload / zero login / zero OAuth. No QR-code login to 3rd-party WOA editors (which carry account-ban risk), no AppID binding, never uploads your unreleased product drafts, confidential internal training articles to any foreign server. All parsing, style assembly, and base64 conversion runs in local JS; meets enterprise WOA content confidentiality requirements.

faqs.q: Will code-block syntax highlighting really survive pasting into WOA? Other tools turned mine into plain black monospace.
faqs.a: Yes, and you have two modes. Option 1 — 'Split into inline-span highlight' (default): every token's color, font size, background, weight is split into inline styles before paste. The WOA editor preserves them verbatim and the WOA client + mobile view are 100% identical; tradeoff is copied rich text payload is slightly larger. Option 2 — 'Use WOA native code-block component': wraps code blocks in the WOA-native <mpcode> component structure so after paste you get WOA's built-in code card; tradeoff is syntax highlight is WOA's default theme, not customizable. We ship Mode 1 by default for color control.

faqs.q: Does URL extraction require me to log into WOA? Will it trigger detection and ban my account?
faqs.a: No login required, no WOA backend APIs touched. As long as it's a publicly-accessible published WOA article URL (one anyone can open in a browser), the tool does a local fetch of the public article HTML then runs regex + DOM parsing — same behavior frequency as a user hitting 'Save As Webpage' in their browser. Fully compliant, zero account risk. Unpublished drafts and backend-only articles obviously can't be extracted because even your own browser can't open them anonymously.

faqs.q: Local images / hotlinked images in my Markdown will display correctly after pasting to WOA?
faqs.a: Three modes: ① Auto convert images to base64 inline (default, most reliable — displays directly in WOA editor on paste, no image bed needed; downside: very large hi-res images make the paste payload heavy, WOA errors out over ~10MB per image). ② Keep original external URLs (only works if your image bed allows WeChat domain referers, otherwise you get broken images). ③ Batch upload into your own WOA material library (click 'Upload images to WOA' button, a WOA backend upload dialog pops up for you to authorize — purely your own backend action, the tool never logs in on your behalf).

faqs.q: Can it restore WOA-native formulas, audio, video, mini-program cards correctly back into Markdown?
faqs.a: Formulas: WOA-native MathML / formula components are restored to LaTeX source ($…$ or $$…$$); formula images restore to image links with alt-text as LaTeX. Audio, video, mini-program cards: since Markdown has no unified rich-media standard, these extract as recognizable custom link blocks (carrying original mp_url / miniprogram appid) so you can identify what they are during re-edit, but they can't be restored back to the exact original WOA card — keep a copy of the raw HTML source if you need round-trip fidelity.

faqs.q: Can it handle an 8000-char + 30-image long article in one go? Will it blow up the browser?
faqs.a: Yes. 8000 chars of Markdown to WOA is effectively instant. With 30 images in 'Convert to base64' mode it takes roughly 5–15 seconds depending on image sizes. If total paste payload exceeds ~20MB the WOA backend will complain the content is too large — at that point switch to 'Text only + keep image URLs' mode, or paste in two batches (upload images separately to the WOA media library), problem solved.

seo.intro: Rare Chinese Character Pinyin Lookup is a free in-browser rare / polyphonic Hanzi reference tool for classical-Chinese enthusiasts, students, parents, publishing editors, and calligraphy learners. Paste anywhere from one to dozens of rare characters, variant forms, or polyphonic Hanzi you don't recognize (simplified / traditional / Kangxi-era forms / Unicode CJK Ext A–G all supported) and the tool returns per character: toned pinyin, ALL polyphonic readings with their matching definitions, radical, stroke count, Unicode codepoint, character structure (left-right / top-bottom / enclosing / undivided), Wubi and Zhengma input codes, top-10 common compounds + 3 classical-source example sentences, homophone and lookalike-character comparisons, plus glyph previews in three script styles (Regular / Clerical / Small Seal Script). It answers the three classic questions: 'What does this read, what does it mean, and how do I type it?'
scenarios: A 4th grader reading a classical Chinese extracurricular book hits 8 rare characters: 饕餮, 貔貅, 囹圄, 龃龉. Dad pastes the 8 chars into the lookup, gets every character's pinyin, radical, compounds, stroke order in 1 second, prints them out and tapes them into the book — saves 20 minutes flipping through 3 paper dictionaries

A classical-text editorial staffer is proofreading a photo-offset Song-dynasty edition of Shiji. Runs into 60+ variant and taboo-avoidance characters. Switches to extended-coverage mode and pastes 50 at a time, verifies Unicode codepoints + Kangxi radical and stroke counts per character, and catches 8 cases where old variant forms map to modern standard characters, avoiding a costly mis-transcription error in the published edition

A guofeng cultural-goods designer is drafting embroidery lettering for a new Hanfu collection with the four classical words 璇玑, 纨素, 氤氲, 潋滟. Pastes them into Lookup to inspect character structure and preview three calligraphic styles, picks the Small Seal Script glyphs to trace into embroidery vector paths — 5× faster than drawing each one by eye.
tutorial: Paste the rare characters you want to look up into the main input. 1 to dozens of chars work fine; simplified, traditional, variant forms, Kangxi-era shapes, Unicode CJK basic + Ext A/B/C/D/E/F/G zones are all supported. Recommend under ~50 chars per query or glyph previews will load slowly.

Toggle options: ① Polyphonic-display mode (most common read only / show all reads with per-reading definitions / prefer ancient pronunciations); ② Lexicon scope (national standard characters only / include extended rare-zone chars / include Kangxi variants); ③ Compound sources (modern Mandarin only / classical texts only / both).

Hit lookup and each character gets its own card. Top: large-size glyph preview (switch between Regular / Clerical / Small Seal Script styles, download single-character PNG vector individually). Below: pinyin incl. all polyphones, radical, stroke count, structure type, Wubi / Zhengma / Unicode, compounds + classical citations. Right side: homophone vs lookalike comparison cards.

Export options: ① Single-character card PNG download (great for flashcards or book inserts); ② Full result export to Excel / CSV (columns: Hanzi, Pinyin, Radical, Strokes, Structure, Compounds, Unicode); ③ Generate an anonymous permanent share link (only uploads the queried char string + results, no personal info).
advantages: Exceptionally wide character-coverage. GB2312 + GBK + GB18030 + Unicode CJK basic + Ext A/B/C/D/E/F/G, over 90 000 total Hanzi fully covered. Reads and radicals resolve for many old variant forms, taboo-avoidance characters, dialect-specific Hanzi, and Japanese / Korean Sinographs that most online dictionaries can't even display. Not one of those useless 6000-common-char-only display dictionaries.

Polyphonic readings are definition-bound. It doesn't just spit a list of pronunciations at you — every reading is attached to the actual usage scenarios and common meanings behind it (for 长, cháng is followed by 'length / long / specialty', zhǎng by 'grow up / leader / to grow'). No more staring at a list of readings and guessing which one fits your sense.

100% browser-local, zero upload. Unpublished classical collation manuscripts from publishers, rare characters on student exams, or prospective trademark names businesses want to register all paste safely. Every codepoint lookup, glyph render, and compound match runs completely locally; your confidential trademark ideas or manuscripts never leave the device.

faqs.q: What's the real difference from a normal online Hanzi dictionary? It looks similar at first.
faqs.a: Three core gaps. ① Coverage: most online dictionaries stop at CJK basic + Ext A (~30 000 chars); we go all the way to Ext G (90 000+) so old variants, dialect chars, Japanese & Korean Sinographs all resolve. ② Batch query: normal dicts do 1 char at a time, we batch up to 50 characters into cards + tables at once — perfect for a whole paragraph of classical text or picture-book unknowns pasted together. ③ Three calligraphic-style previews (Regular / Clerical / Small Seal) with direct per-char PNG vector download for creative / calligraphy / embroidery workflows — normal dictionaries have none of that.

faqs.q: Does it show simplified ↔ traditional ↔ variant mappings? Like 體 → 体.
faqs.a: Yes. Every card's 'Lookalikes / Correspondences' section lists bidirectional mappings: simplified ↔ traditional, standard character ↔ variant form, new printed form ↔ old printed form (looking up 體 will show simplified 体 plus variants 骵 / 軆). A global Simp / Trad toggle switches the whole result display in one click too.

faqs.q: Can it show stroke-order animations for teaching kids to write?
faqs.a: Absolutely. Each card's top-right has a 'Stroke Order' button — clicking it plays a standard stroke-order animation (following the National Language Commission's 'Modern Chinese Common Character Stroke Order Standard'). You can step through stroke-by-stroke, auto-loop, or export as an animated MP4 or per-frame PNG sequence. Great for teaching kids or calligraphy beginners.

faqs.q: Are the compounds and example sentences accurate? No AI-hallucinated nonsense words?
faqs.a: Compounds and sentences draw from two public authoritative corpora: modern Mandarin uses BCC Corpus + *Modern Chinese Dictionary* 7th-ed alignments; classical uses Siku Quanshu full-text search + high-frequency word alignment from Guwen Guanzhi and the first four histories of the Shiji canon. No AI-invented fake compounds. Every example sentence is tagged with its source (which book, which chapter) so you can verify independently.

faqs.q: I'm trademark-clearing a rare character name — does it show GB18030 or Unicode codepoints?
faqs.a: Yes. Every single card lists four encodings: Unicode codepoint (U+XXXX), GB18030 byte sequence, raw UTF-8 bytes, and Wubi 86 / 98 input codes. It also explicitly flags whether the character is inside the *Table of General Standard Chinese Characters* (8105 chars) and whether it's in the Level-1 (3500 most common) subset — exactly the checks trademark clerks and namers run to confirm a character is 'standard' enough for registration.

faqs.q: Is what I generate private?

faqs.q: Will it work on my phone?

faqs.q: Can I suggest or add new excuse lines?

name-constellation.name: Name Constellation
name-constellation.description: Transform your name into a unique star-map personality profile. Each letter becomes a star. AI reveals your personality traits, lucky color, and lucky...

seo.intro: Name Constellation is a free, browser-based creative tool that transforms your name into a one-of-a-kind star-map personality profile. Each letter shines as a star in your personal constellation. AI uncovers the energy meaning of each letter, your personality traits, lucky color, and lucky number. Everything runs locally in your browser — no data uploads, no account needed.
scenarios: Personal avatars and social media cards — use your unique star map as a distinctive profile picture.
Birthday and anniversary gifts — generate star maps for friends or loved ones, pair with a frame for a meaningful gift.
Social icebreaker — share your constellation on social platforms and spark conversations with personality readings.
Self-exploration and meditation — understand your personality traits and energy distribution through your star map.
Couple / best-friend comparison — overlay two star maps to see if your energies complement each other.
tutorial: Step 1: Enter your name in the input box (supports any language).
Step 2: Choose a galaxy style — Milky Way, Aurora, Twilight, or Dreamscape.
Step 3: Click "Generate Star Map" and AI will create your unique constellation.
Step 4: Drag to pan, scroll to zoom, click individual stars to see letter meanings.
Step 5: Click "Download PNG" to save your star map, or "Regenerate" for a new reading.
advantages: 100% browser-based. Your name and star map data never leave your device.
AI-powered deep reading — not just visuals, but personality traits, lucky color, and lucky number analysis.
Four beautiful styles. Every name generates a unique constellation, never repeated.
Completely free with unlimited generations. No sign-up, no watermarks.
Supports six languages for input and interface — built for global users.

faqs.q: Is Name Constellation free?
faqs.a: Yes, completely free. All features — AI reading, four styles, PNG export — are permanently free with no hidden paywalls.

faqs.q: Do I need to create an account?
faqs.a: No. Works instantly in any browser. No email, no login, no tracking cookies.

faqs.q: Is my name data uploaded?
faqs.a: No. Core rendering happens locally in your browser. AI reading requests are anonymous and don't store personal information.

faqs.q: What devices are supported?
faqs.a: Works on all modern browsers (Chrome, Edge, Safari, Firefox) across PC, tablet, and mobile. Touch controls are optimized for mobile.

faqs.q: Can I generate the same name multiple times?
faqs.a: Yes. Each generation is unique — AI creates different readings and star layouts for the same name.

image-pdf-converter.name: Image to PDF / PDF to Image Converter
image-pdf-converter.description: Combine multiple images into a PDF or export each PDF page as PNG/JPG locally in your browser.

seo.intro: This browser-based image and PDF converter does two things in one place: it merges multiple JPG/PNG/WebP images into a single PDF, with customizable page size, orientation and margins; and it can also take a PDF and render every page into a PNG or JPG image for individual export. Everything runs locally on your device, so neither your images nor your PDFs — contracts, IDs, invoices or any sensitive documents — are ever uploaded to the cloud.
scenarios: Combine photos of IDs, licenses or contracts into a single PDF for submission or email attachment
Export each page of a product brochure or research paper PDF as images for sharing, slides or social media posts
Build a printable album PDF from travel photos using a standard paper size
Extract charts and figures from a report PDF as images to paste into documents or decks
tutorial: Pick the mode: Images to PDF, or PDF to Images.
For Images to PDF: upload several pictures, reorder them by dragging, then set page size, orientation and margins.
For PDF to Images: upload a PDF and choose the output format (PNG or JPG) and render quality.
Generate, preview, then download files individually or in bulk.
advantages: Fully local execution: neither your images nor the PDF ever touch a remote server.
Two-way capability in a single tool: assemble PDFs from images, and explode PDFs back into images.
Supports common paper sizes (A4, Letter, A5) and landscape/portrait to fit standard printing and submission workflows.

faqs.q: Are my PDFs and images uploaded to the cloud?
faqs.a: No. All reading, rendering and composing happen inside your browser; nothing leaves your device.

faqs.q: How do I choose a page size for the generated PDF?
faqs.a: Choose between A4, Letter, A5, the original image dimensions, and a few other options depending on your paper or workflow.

faqs.q: Will text in the exported PDF pages look blurry?
faqs.a: The default quality is a balanced medium; raise the DPI/quality slider for sharper renders if you are willing to accept larger file sizes.

faqs.q: Can I export a multi-page PDF into multiple images?
faqs.a: Yes. The tool generates one image per page; download them one by one or all at once.

faqs.q: How is this different from the PDF merger?
faqs.a: The PDF merger works with PDFs on both sides. This tool specializes in converting between image formats and PDF. They complement each other nicely.

json-csv-converter.name: JSON to CSV / CSV to JSON Converter
json-csv-converter.description: Two-way JSON ↔ CSV conversion in your browser. Supports nested JSON flattening, custom delimiters, copy and file download.

seo.intro: This online JSON ↔ CSV converter quickly transforms a JSON array into a CSV table, or a CSV table back into a standard JSON array of objects, all inside your browser. Deeply nested JSON objects can be automatically flattened using a custom key separator of your choice, and the same separator can un-flatten dotted column names (like address.city) back into nested objects on the way back. Parsing and export are fully local, so customer lists, user exports, API responses and other sensitive data never get sent to a remote server.
scenarios: Turn an API JSON response into CSV for pivot tables and charts in Excel, Numbers or Sheets
Import a marketing or operations CSV export into scripts and pipelines as structured JSON
Flatten complex nested JSON into a simple CSV so it loads into relational databases or BI tools
Grab a JSON payload while debugging a backend, paste it here and export a shareable table for teammates
tutorial: Choose the direction: JSON → CSV or CSV → JSON. Default sample contents are swapped for you.
Paste your input into the left editor.
Tune the options: flatten nested JSON, pick a CSV delimiter, and set the key separator for nesting.
The right panel updates in real time; copy the output or download it as a file.
advantages: Two-way conversion with nested flattening and un-flattening, all in one place.
Everything runs in the browser. Your CSV and JSON data never leave your machine.
Multiple CSV delimiters out of the box (comma, semicolon, Tab, pipe), including the formats used in German-speaking regions.

faqs.q: Will my data leave my computer?
faqs.a: No. Parsing, conversion and export happen completely in the browser; nothing is posted over the network.

faqs.q: How do you handle nested JSON?
faqs.a: By default the flattening option is on, so deep keys become dotted columns like address.city. On the reverse direction the same separator rebuilds the nested structure.

faqs.q: What about array fields?
faqs.a: Arrays are serialized as JSON strings inside the cell by default, so information is not lost. Expand them manually into columns if you need a wider table.

faqs.q: Which CSV delimiters are supported?
faqs.a: Comma, semicolon, Tab and the pipe symbol — covering the most common spreadsheet export variants.

faqs.q: How is this different from the JSON formatter?
faqs.a: The JSON formatter focuses on pretty-printing, validation and minification. This tool focuses on bidirectional conversion between JSON and tabular CSV. Use them together.
